newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn coalition seen retreating from bold tax goals.
newsitem.headline: Bonn coalition seen retreating from bold tax goals.

text.p: Germany's beleaguered coalition, by agreeing on changes to ambitious tax reforms, has papered over the cracks opened by its frenetic efforts to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

But, analysts said on Friday, the redrawn reform of the tax system approved by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition late on Thursday retreats from its earlier tax-cutting goals and risks being watered down further in parliament.
"It is still a clear improvement on the status quo, but unfortunately not the bold leap that was originally envisaged," Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs, said.
"Such reforms simply may not be possible in this country."

By amending Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to shake up the German tax system to try to make it more palatable to the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), the coalition appears to have satisfied nobody.
Business lobbies attacked new restrictions on corporate loss-carryovers by saying they would put extra burdens on firms now paying one of the highest marginal rates of tax in Europe.
"Companies...must not be asked yet again to pay the bill," Michael Fuchs, head of the BGA trade and wholesale group, said.

The new proposal also backs off scrapping at a stroke tax relief on anti-social work hours, instead phasing it out by 2003. But the SPD, which can veto the tax reform in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament, said the changes did not go far enough for it to drop its tax blockade.

And, although the three parties in the Kohl coalition gave their backing to the amended tax reform, sniping resumed from the wings against the embattled Waigel, who is still struggling to contain borrowing and make the grade for EMU.
Waigel's original tax draft had planned to cut income and corporate taxes, scrap tax breaks and simplify the complex tax system to give Germany's jobless-hit economy a boost.
The government has pulled back on all those fronts, and Mayer said he expected the net relief to taxpayers now to fall short of the 30 billion marks originally targeted by Waigel.
Economist Holger Fahrinkrug at UBS in Frankfurt agreed that Waigel's tax-cutting goal had never been realistic because of the seriousness of Germany's budget problems.
"It's just castles in the air," Fahrinkrug said. "When someone says he wants to cut 30 billion marks in taxes in the foreseeable future, I just don't believe him."
The amended tax reform legislation will be put to the Bundestag lower house of parliament for final readings on June 26, and should be passed with the government's slim majority.

The bills, which would phase in the tax changes in 1998 and 1999, then go into the Bundesrat where they face certain defeat at the hands of the SPD. Then, from mid-July the horse-trading with the SPD will start in parliamentary mediation.

With the tax reform issue out of the way for now, Waigel faces four weeks of hard bargaining within Kohl's three-party alliance to plug gaps in the 1997 and 1998 budgets to try to hit the budget deficit target set by the Maastricht treaty.
Analysts said they did not expect Waigel to achieve his stated deficit goal of 3.0 percent of gross domestic product this year while abiding by a coalition deal not to raise taxes.
Putting together a budget for 1998 by the coalition's July 11 deadline may be even harder, with big spending projects like the Eurofighter combat jet hanging in the balance.

But analysts did not expect the coalition to fail, since no other constellation -- including early elections -- would improve the lot of the Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Free Democrats (FDP) who make up Kohl's 14-year-old coalition.
"I don't see a chance to reach 3.0," Mayer said. "But all other options are unattractive. That's why I think the coalition will just keep muddling along."
